cards.title: The Mirror Formula
cards.body: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f — where u is object distance, v is image distance, and f is focal length. For a concave mirror f is positive; for convex f is negative. All distances measured from the pole of the mirror.

cards.title: Linear Magnification
cards.body: m = −v/u. The sign matters! Negative m means the image is inverted. |m| > 1 means magnified; |m| < 1 means diminished. An upright virtual image always has m > 0.

cards.title: The Concave Mirror
cards.body: A concave mirror curves inward — like the inside of a bowl. It bends incoming rays toward a focal point F in front of the mirror. f is positive. Used in torches, telescopes, and dentist's mirrors.

cards.title: The Convex Mirror
cards.body: A convex mirror curves outward. Rays always diverge — so it always forms a smaller, upright, virtual image. f is negative. Used in rear-view mirrors and security mirrors for their wide field of view.

cards.title: Object Position Changes Everything
cards.body: F and C (= 2F) divide the space in front of a concave mirror into three regions. Object beyond C → diminished real image. Object between F and C → magnified real image. Object inside F → magnified virtual image.

cards.title: Real vs Virtual Images
cards.body: Real image: reflected rays actually converge — v is positive, image is inverted, can be projected on screen. Virtual image: rays diverge — v is negative, image appears behind mirror, upright, cannot be projected.

cards.title: How to Play
cards.body: Drag the white arrow left or right to move the object. The image updates live. Some missions ask you to predict what will happen before you experiment. Formula missions ask you to calculate v and m — enter your answers below the diagram.

missions.title: Real Image — Guided
missions.learningGoal: Discover that a concave mirror forms a real image when the object is placed beyond the focal point.

payload.hint: Drag the object to the LEFT, past F. A real image forms when the object is beyond the focal point.

missions.title: Predict: Where Does a Real Image Form?
missions.learningGoal: Predict where to place an object to get a real image, then verify by experimenting.

payload.hint: Keep the object beyond F (to the left of F) to get a real image.

prediction.question: A student wants to get a REAL image using a concave mirror. Where should they place the object?
options: Inside F — between the mirror and the focal point
Beyond F — further from the mirror than the focal point
It doesn't matter where the object is placed
Behind the mirror
prediction.explanation: For a real image in a concave mirror, the object must be beyond F. Reflected rays then converge in front of the mirror, forming a real image that can be projected on a screen. When the object is inside F, rays diverge — producing only a virtual image.

missions.title: Predict: Inside F
missions.learningGoal: Predict that moving an object inside F gives a virtual, magnified, upright image.

payload.hint: Move the object to the RIGHT, inside F. Rays will diverge and a virtual, magnified image appears behind the mirror.

prediction.question: If you move the object INSIDE the focal point F of a concave mirror, what kind of image will you see?
options: A real, inverted, magnified image in front of the mirror
No image at all
A virtual, upright, magnified image appearing behind the mirror
A real, upright image at C
prediction.explanation: When the object is inside F, reflected rays diverge — they never meet in front of the mirror. But extended backward, they appear to meet behind the mirror. The result is a virtual, upright, magnified image. This is how a makeup mirror or dentist's mirror works.

missions.title: Predict: The Convex Mirror
missions.learningGoal: Predict that a convex mirror always produces a virtual, upright, diminished image regardless of object position.

payload.hint: A convex mirror always forms a virtual image — it doesn't matter where the object is. Try moving it around to confirm.

prediction.question: A convex mirror is used as a rear-view mirror. What kind of image does it ALWAYS produce, regardless of where the object is?
options: A real, inverted image — like a camera
A virtual, upright, smaller image — seeing more of the scene
A virtual, inverted image — objects appear upside down
A real image only when the object is far away
prediction.explanation: A convex mirror always diverges reflected rays — they never converge. So the image is always virtual (behind the mirror), upright, and smaller than the object. The advantage is a wider field of view, which is why convex mirrors are used in vehicles and shops.

missions.title: Predict: Getting a Bigger Image
missions.learningGoal: Predict that placing the object between F and C produces a magnified real image.

payload.hint: Place the object between F and C. The closer to F, the bigger the real image.

prediction.question: You want a MAGNIFIED real image using a concave mirror. Where should you position the object?
options: Beyond C — more than twice the focal length from the mirror
At C — exactly twice the focal length from the mirror
Between F and C — between one and two focal lengths from the mirror
Inside F — less than one focal length from the mirror
prediction.explanation: Between F and C is the magnified real image zone. The image forms beyond C on the same side as the object and is inverted and larger. At C, the image is the same size. Beyond C, the image is smaller. Inside F, you only get a virtual image.

missions.title: Predict: Object at C
missions.learningGoal: Predict that an object at C produces a real, inverted image of the same size also at C.

payload.hint: Place the object at C — the marker labelled C on the axis. The image will also form at C and be the same size.

prediction.question: If you place the object at the Centre of Curvature C (where C = 2F), what image do you expect?
options: A magnified real image beyond C
A virtual image behind the mirror
A real, inverted image of the same size, also at C
No image — object at C means no reflection
prediction.explanation: When u = 2f (object at C), the mirror formula gives v = 2f as well. So the image also forms at C, is real, inverted, and the same size as the object (m = −1). This is a special symmetric case — useful in optical instruments to re-image an object in the same plane.

missions.title: Real Image — Master
missions.learningGoal: Apply the mirror formula to produce exactly 2× magnification with no labels as guides.

payload.hint: For 2× magnification: v = 2u, and from 1/v + 1/u = 1/f → u = 1.5f. Count grid lines to estimate position.

missions.title: Virtual Image — Master
missions.learningGoal: Produce a precisely diminished virtual image using a convex mirror with no labels.

payload.hint: Convex mirror, object far from the mirror — the further away, the smaller the virtual image.

missions.title: Mirror Formula — First Calculation
missions.learningGoal: Apply 1/v + 1/u = 1/f and m = −v/u to calculate image distance and magnification.

payload.hint: Place the object at C (2F). Then use 1/v = 1/f − 1/u to find v, and m = −v/u to find m.

prediction.question: Before calculating: if u = 2f, what do you expect v and |m| to be?
options: v = f, |m| = 0.5 (image at F, half-size)
v = 2f, |m| = 1 (image at C, same size)
v = ∞ (no image — object at C causes infinity)
v = 3f, |m| = 1.5 (image beyond C, magnified)
prediction.explanation: When u = 2f: 1/v = 1/f − 1/2f = 1/2f, so v = 2f. And m = −v/u = −2f/2f = −1. The image is at C, same size, inverted. Now use the formula with the actual u shown on the diagram to confirm.

missions.title: Mirror Formula — Magnified Image
missions.learningGoal: Calculate v and m for a magnified real image using the mirror formula.

payload.hint: Place the object between F and C. Note the u value shown on the diagram, then calculate 1/v = 1/f − 1/u.

missions.title: Magnification Challenge
missions.learningGoal: Calculate linear magnification m = −v/u, including the correct sign.

payload.hint: m = −v/u. Read the v value shown below the image arrow. The sign matters — it tells you if the image is upright (+) or inverted (−).

prediction.question: What does a NEGATIVE value of m tell you about the image?
options: The image is virtual
The image is inverted (upside down)
The image is smaller than the object
The mirror is convex
prediction.explanation: The sign of m tells you orientation only. Negative m → inverted image. Positive m → upright image. The magnitude |m| tells you size — whether the image is bigger or smaller than the object. A virtual image always has m positive (upright), but a real image always has m negative (inverted).

missions.title: Dentist's Mirror
missions.learningGoal: Understand why a dentist's mirror produces a magnified upright virtual image of teeth.

payload.hint: A dentist's mirror is concave, held so the tooth is inside F. Move the object inside F to see the magnified upright virtual image.

prediction.question: A dentist holds a concave mirror close to a tooth — closer than the focal point F. What image will they see?
options: A real, inverted image projected in the air
A magnified, upright virtual image appearing behind the mirror
No image — object too close for a concave mirror
A diminished upright image
prediction.explanation: When the object (tooth) is inside F, reflected rays diverge and appear to come from a point behind the mirror. The dentist sees a magnified, upright virtual image — making small details like cavities much easier to inspect.

missions.title: Rear-View Mirror
missions.learningGoal: Explain why a convex rear-view mirror gives a wide field of view but makes objects look smaller.

payload.hint: Move the object far from the convex mirror to simulate a car far behind. The image gets smaller but you can still see it — this is the wide field of view.

prediction.question: Why do rear-view mirrors in cars say 'Objects in mirror are closer than they appear'?
options: Because the mirror is slightly tinted, reducing clarity
Because convex mirrors make objects appear smaller, so they seem further away than they really are
Because real images in concave mirrors are always inverted
Because the glass adds a delay to the reflection
prediction.explanation: A convex mirror always produces a smaller virtual image. Because the image is smaller, your brain interprets the object as being further away than it actually is. This is why the warning label exists — the car behind you is actually closer than the small image suggests.

missions.title: Telescope Mirror
missions.learningGoal: Produce a large real image as a concave reflecting telescope mirror would for a distant star.

payload.hint: Place the object just outside F — this produces the largest real image. A telescope's eyepiece would be placed at the image position to magnify it further.
